title: Which accounting jobs can software do, and which still need a person?
description: Of the 16 accounting jobs in the library's map, software working from reliable event records can do 6 strongly: identity; authority; settlement; internal control; reconciliation; correction and recovery. Three more are strong once a condition holds: classification, when facts are complete; allocation, for fixed rules; reporting and disclosure, after judgments. Six can be done only partly: entity and perimeter; occurrence / existence; rights and obligations; recognition; close and consolidation; assurance. Measurement is mixed. The map's rule of thumb: the closer a function is to identity, authorization, arithmetic, sequencing and reconciliation, the more programmable it is. The closer it is to economic substance, legal rights, uncertain measurement and materiality, the more judgment remains.
search_context: accounting-software-limits line-up innovation

title: How are big banks limiting group lawsuits in their customer contracts?
description: Through their customer agreements: across 12 dated records from November 2018 to June 4, 2026, the library documents 8 banks and card issuers (Bank of America, Bread / Comenity, Chase, Citi, Cross River, PNC, Synchrony, Truist) using individual arbitration, waivers of class and group claims, and short mailed opt-out windows, and 3 records add special rules for mass filings. Each card links the contract or notice it comes from.
search_context: bank-arbitration timeline banking

title: Which private shared-ledger settlement networks settle in central-bank money?
description: Of the 12 market-infrastructure systems in the library, 1 is recorded as settling in central-bank money: the Sterling Fnality Payment System, run by Fnality UK Ltd (supervised by the Bank of England). 4 move banks' own tokenized deposits, which are commercial-bank money, and for the other 7 the library does not say what money they settle in.
search_context: bank-central-bank-money line-up banking

title: Who really owns your loan?
description: Often not the bank or brand you see. In Affirm's program agreements filed with the SEC (November 2020), Cross River Bank is the named lender, Affirm buys most of the loans, owns the customer information and services them, and Upstart processes applications and keeps the register of who owns the note. On the library's July 11, 2026 reading, the Affirm Card is issued by Evolve or Stride, not Cross River, and Upstart's note permits sale without borrower consent and discloses the owner only on written request.
search_context: bank-loan-owner entity chart banking

title: Has the federal government really stopped sending paper checks?
description: Mostly, not entirely. Executive Order 14247 (signed March 25, 2025 · published March 28, 2025) ordered an end to paper checks for federal payments, and a customs notice of July 8, 2026 says the government no longer sends them; but the Treasury's own April 29, 2026 proposal still sets out when agencies may send one, and the PBGC was moving its remaining paper-check recipients on June 24, 2026. In FY2026 Treasury screened >1.1 billion payment requests (about $3.7 trillion) before the money went out.
search_context: bank-paper-checks timeline banking

title: Did the ban on 'reputation risk' debanking become law, and at which agencies?
description: It became agency regulation, not a law passed by Congress: the OCC and FDIC adopted a final rule (April 10, 2026); the NCUA adopted a final rule (June 25, 2026); the Federal Reserve Board has only proposed one (February 26, 2026). The NCUA's rule says it implements Executive Order 14331 (signed August 7, 2025 · published August 12, 2025).
search_context: bank-reputation-risk scorecard banking

title: What changes in your card or bank contract when your bank is sold?
description: The library follows 6 bank sales and card-program moves since April 1, 2025 (Ally / Merrick, Capital One / Discover, Goldman, Fifth Third, Bilt / Column, PNC). In each, the brand, card number or app stays while the legal bank behind it changes, and the customer's new terms arrive on a separate, later clock; 2 conversions (Fifth Third, Goldman) have no customer contract published yet.
search_context: bank-sold-contract timeline banking

title: Which big banks have live tokenized deposits or deposit tokens?
description: 4 of the 16 big institutions in the library have tokenized deposits or deposit tokens in use: J.P. Morgan, Citi, BNY and HSBC. The rest are piloting, have announced plans, or show nothing yet. 3 of the 16 are asset managers, not banks.
search_context: bank-tokenized-deposits grid banking

title: What has each card network and payment company actually launched with stablecoins?
description: Of 32 stablecoin products from card networks and payment companies, 11 are fully live and 10 are live on a limited basis. 5 are pilots and 2 are announced only. In most live products the customer spends stablecoins while the shop is paid in ordinary money.
search_context: card-network-stablecoins line-up crypto

title: Where does the CLARITY market-structure bill stand, draft by draft?
description: It is not law. The CLARITY Act (H.R. 3633) passed the House, and Senate sponsors released three public drafts: EHF26654 (616 pages, July 22, 2026), EHF26718 (630 pages, September 10, 2026) and EHF26724 (635 pages, September 14, 2026). None was formally filed as an amendment. On September 15, 2026 the Senate voted 49 to 50 on taking the bill up, short of the 60 votes needed, and the library's web check on October 19, 2026 found no later step.
search_context: clarity-drafts timeline crypto

title: Which countries license stablecoins, and what must back them?
description: The library tracks 22 jurisdictions. Each card says who must license a stablecoin issuer there, what has to back the coin and what holders can claim, and which issuers are actually operating.
search_context: country-stablecoin-rules map crypto

title: Can a CPA license make you an accredited investor?
description: Not yet. On September 30, 2026 the SEC issued Release 33-11446, a notice and request for comment on a possible designation order under Rule 501(a)(10) of Regulation D: a natural person holding an active U.S. CPA license in good standing would qualify personally as an accredited investor, without the income or net-worth tests. It is not a final order; comments are due 60 days after Federal Register publication, and that date was not yet set when the library last checked (October 5, 2026). What a CPA can do today is give a Rule 506(c) written confirmation that another investor is accredited.
search_context: cpa-accredited-investor steps banking

title: If you want dollars back from a stablecoin or tokenized fund, who pays you, how fast, and what can stop it?
description: It depends on the route, and only the proposed federal rule names a speed. Of the 7 routes the library compares, the issuer or fund pays you back for USDC (Circle, for eligible holders) and USYC (Circle's USDC Teller, whose available liquidity is shown in real time; larger and same-day requests go through support procedures). For BUIDL, the routes are an announced exchange of fund shares for Ripple's RLUSD and trades with whitelisted counterparties on UniswapX, which gives "no assurance of liquidity or pricing." On CHIPS, XRPL and Swift it is participant positions, trading liquidity or banks. What can stop you: holder eligibility, verification, jurisdiction and bank payout timing for USDC; undisclosed bank terms on Swift; withdrawal rules on CHIPS. The Fed's proposal would give issuers no more than 2 business days to redeem after a valid request; it is not final.
search_context: crypto-cash-out-routes line-up crypto

title: Where does each crypto firm stand in the bank-charter line?
description: 6 crypto and fintech firms are open as chartered banks and 1 more has final approval. 15 hold conditional approvals and 11 are waiting on applications; 1 was denied.
search_context: crypto-charters line-up crypto

title: When a crypto firm collapsed, did its customers get their money back, and how?
description: Rarely in full. Of 10 cases the library tracks, customers are being paid back, at least partly, in 3 (Cryptopia liquidation, Mt. Gox civil rehabilitation, FTX Chapter 11 distribution), no payout is confirmed in the library's record for 5, and 1 recovered everything (Wuhan virtual-currency cash-out fraud). How much comes back depends on whether a court treats customer crypto as the customers' own property held in trust or as the failed firm's assets.
search_context: crypto-collapses line-up crypto

title: What does each crypto company control, where can it stop a payment, and how does it make money?
description: Each controls a different step around the coin, not just the coin. Issuers (Circle, Ripple's Standard Custody, Tether, Paxos, Agora) decide who can mint and redeem, and Tether, Standard Custody and Agora can also freeze tokens; Coinbase and Stripe control listings, accounts and which payments qualify; Anchorage's bank can refuse minting or redemption and freeze or seize tokens under its product terms, while Fireblocks' transfer rules are set by its customers. Issuers earn mostly reserve income (Circle: $652.5 million in the first quarter of 2026, with $405.4 million of distribution and transaction costs); distributors and service firms earn fees.
search_context: crypto-company-control line-up crypto

title: Which cross-border crypto payment routes between countries actually work today?
description: None counts yet. Of the 15 cross-border routes the International Crypto Map reviewed (evidence through October 3, 2026), it draws none as a working crypto payment route. 5 had live payments (UAE-China mBridge payment and later Jisr launch, Swift ledger multicontinent tokenized-value payments, ANZ-BHP-Citi Swift-ledger Melbourne-New York payments, DBS-Citi live USD Swift-ledger transactions and UOB-HSBC live HKD Swift-ledger transactions), but each lacks a complete record of who paid whom, the final settlement and the receiver's credit. 2 work every day but move ordinary bank money, not crypto (Indonesia-Japan QR payment linkage and Hong Kong-Mainland China Payment Connect). The other 8 are products, permissions, tests or research with no payment shown.
search_context: crypto-cross-border-routes map world

title: Which crypto networks and companies would the Fed's stablecoin rules reach, and how?
description: The Federal Reserve Board's two GENIUS Act proposals of September 24, 2026 reach the 20 crypto networks and companies the library maps in four different ways: 2 would face them directly as stablecoin issuers (Ripple / XRPL and Circle / USDC / CPN / Arc / Tazapay); 4 as custody, distribution or payout services (Securitize, Cash legs & tokenized bank money, Coinbase / Base / Tokenize and SWIFT ledger & bank obligations); 12 as technical systems an issuer would run on; and 2 sit outside the direct issuer rules (Bitcoin and DTC / DTCC tokenization). The proposals are not final, and they approve no company, network or token.
search_context: crypto-fed-rules-reach grid crypto

title: Which license does each job in a tokenized market need, and which firms hold one?
description: Each of the 26 jobs in a tokenized market has at least one legal route. The library maps 52 routes, each with its legal basis, the conditions and its limit, and names 57 firms or public bodies documented on them. A license covers the exact company that holds it and the activity it names; a technology vendor or parent company does not inherit it.
search_context: crypto-licenses line-up crypto

title: Who has legal authority over each part of the U.S. securities and payments plumbing?
description: No single body. The library maps 89 U.S. laws, agencies, market bodies and failure-handling roles, joined by 96 recorded legal links; 37 of them are the market institutions, accounts and settlement services themselves. The agencies with the most supervisory links into market institutions and settlement services are Securities and Exchange Commission (12), Commodity Futures Trading Commission (7) and Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System (5). The Financial Stability Oversight Council designated 8 utilities as systemically important (CLS Bank International, Chicago Mercantile Exchange, DTC, FICC, ICE Clear Credit, NSCC, Options Clearing Corporation and The Clearing House Payments Company); under Title VIII each has a supervisory agency: Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System for The Clearing House Payments Company and CLS Bank International; Commodity Futures Trading Commission for Chicago Mercantile Exchange and ICE Clear Credit; Securities and Exchange Commission for DTC, NSCC, FICC and Options Clearing Corporation. DTC alone answers to 4: Financial Stability Oversight Council (designates), Securities and Exchange Commission (Title VIII supervisory agency), New York Department of Financial Services (state trust supervision) and Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System (state member bank supervision).
search_context: crypto-plumbing-authority grid banking

title: What does each blockchain network, DeFi protocol and yield product control, where can it stop a payment, and how does it make money?
description: Very different amounts. On Ethereum, validators can censor or leave out transactions; on Stellar and Hedera each token's issuer sets its own freeze controls. Aave, Sky and Curve can change settings, caps or fees by governance vote, but Liquity's core design has no way to pause, upgrade or blacklist. Ethena and Ondo control who may mint and redeem; Morpho's governance cannot pause existing markets, while its vault curators choose where lenders' money goes. They earn from network fees, borrowing interest and protocol fees, and Ethena from derivatives funding payments.
search_context: crypto-protocol-control line-up crypto

title: What must a tokenized system prove before it can be trusted with real money, and which systems pass each test?
description: No system is shown to pass yet. The library's 14-part readiness test, saved September 22, 2026, asks what a tokenized system must prove, from a legally defined claim to final money and the retirement of old systems, and rates 34 systems on fit only: in its words, "Functional fit is not legal qualification." The strongest candidates are DTC / DTCC tokenization (core on 7), Circle / USDC / CPN / Arc / Tazapay (core on 6) and Securitize (core on 6). No system is a core candidate for test 14, Economics and legacy retirement.
search_context: crypto-readiness-tests grid crypto

title: At which step of a trade or payment does a crypto company actually replace a bank, broker or registrar?
description: At none of them, on the library's walk-through. Across 3 everyday processes (buying a broker-held share, making a dollar payment, subscribing to a fund), 17 steps and 46 seats, the answer to "does it take over?" is No every time. It notes a crypto overlap at 39 seats, meaning "a different claim, a membership, or a software path hanging off the same rail": for example, DTC tokenization can re-represent a participant's entitlement, and Securitize, LLC is the transfer agent for BlackRock's BUIDL fund, a seat it holds "by appointment, not by replacing the fund." In each case the books that count stay with the bank, broker, depository or registrar.
search_context: crypto-replace-bank-step every record crypto

title: Which crypto rules are final, which are only proposals, and what does each one actually allow?
description: Of the 8 crypto rules, orders and bills the library tracks outside the GENIUS Act, 2 are in effect, 3 are formal proposals, 1 is still at the advance-notice stage, 1 is non-binding staff guidance, and the one market-structure bill, the CLARITY Act, is blocked: the Senate fell short of the 60 votes needed to take it up on September 15, 2026. None of the proposals is final yet.
search_context: crypto-rules line-up crypto

title: What do 'settled' and 'final' really mean for an ACH payment, a tokenized stock and a DTC token?
description: They mean different things in each system, and "final" in one record does not settle the others. ACH: The Reserve Bank debits the sending bank and credits the receiving bank at the scheduled time. For a credit item, the receiving bank's settlement credit is final and available under Operating Circular 4. Securitize tokenized stock: The product is designed to exchange the CET and USDC atomically on Solana. Solana can make the token transfer technically confirmed while Securitize determines the governed entitlement state. DTC token: The entitlement representation moves between registered participant wallets free of value. DTC's official record recognizes the participant wallet location of the entitlement.
search_context: crypto-settled-final grid banking

title: When you buy into BlackRock's BUIDL fund, send USDC or buy a tokenized share, which company is responsible at each step?
description: A different company at almost every step, and the money step is mostly unmapped. In a BUIDL subscription, Securitize Markets, LLC gives eligible investors access, the fund (BlackRock USD Institutional Digital Liquidity Fund Ltd.) issues the shares, Securitize, LLC keeps the share register, and The Bank of New York Mellon must confirm the subscription money first. For USDC, Circle Internet Financial, LLC is the issuer behind each documented step, but a token transfer alone is not a bank payout. For the Coinbase tokenized share, Coinbase Onchain SPV Ltd issues the certificate, Alpaca Securities LLC holds the underlying Apple share, Base carries the token and Onchain Marketplace Limited keeps the Legal Register that decides ownership. Across the three, 10 of 12 money steps are not mapped in the library's evidence.
search_context: crypto-who-does-each-step grid crypto

title: Who is where, and how far along?
description: 416 companies, banks, coins, networks and systems, each placed at the legal-entity level: 178 entity-on-network statuses with their history, 747 process roles, 198 legal lanes, 362 country links and 262 dated steps. Pick any entity to see what it owns, what it is only connected to, and where each of its companies stands.
search_context: crypto-who-is-where explorer crypto

title: Where does the drone beyond-visual-line-of-sight rule (Part 108) stand, and what other drone rules are pending?
description: Part 108 is still only a proposal: the FAA and TSA proposed it August 7, 2025, refused more comment time September 29, 2025 and reopened comments on one design question January 28, 2026; the record holds no final rule, although EO 14307 set a 240-day final-rule target ('as appropriate'). The other pending drone rule is the FAA's May 6, 2026 proposal to restrict drones near fixed-site facilities (comments extended to August 5, 2026). 3 items are notices, not rules: Electric Vertical Takeoff and Landing and Advanced Air Mobility Integration Pilot Program — Establishment and Request for Proposals; Implementing Section 927 Waiver Process for Certain Unmanned Aircraft Operations; Unleashing American Drone Dominance (FCC Notice of Inquiry). 2 are final: Integration of Powered-Lift: Pilot Certification and Operations (SFAR); Streamlining Export Controls for Drone Exports.
search_context: drone-rules timeline innovation

title: Is DTC's tokenization live, and on which blockchains?
description: Partly. DTC ran its first production trades with tokenized assets on July 15, 2026, in a limited form. As of October 19, 2026, DTCC still describes the full service as an October 2026 launch and has not announced it. Blockchains named: LFDT Besu (DTCC's private network) (live, limited, since 2026-07-15), Canton Network (public) (live, limited, since 2026-07-15), Stellar (public) (announced only, expected first half of 2027), Arc (Circle) (announced only, expected 2027).
search_context: dtc-tokenization timeline crypto

title: Which federal agencies does each executive order put to work?
description: The 509 Trump executive orders with agency maps (January 20, 2017 to September 29, 2026) put 163 federal agencies and offices to work. The Justice Department is named in the most orders (153), then the Office of Management and Budget (147) and the Department of Homeland Security (139).
search_context: eo-agencies bars + tree institutions

title: What have courts decided about who gets a Fed account?
description: So far the courts side with the Fed. Two appeals courts (the Tenth Circuit for Custodia in 2025 and the Second Circuit for Banco San Juan in 2026) held that being eligible for a Fed account does not entitle a bank to one. Custodia has asked the Supreme Court to take the case, and the Fed opposed review on October 13, 2026.
search_context: fed-account-courts timeline banking

title: Master account, limited account or payment account: what is the difference?
description: A master account gives full access to the Fed's payment services and its credit. A limited-purpose account (so far only Kraken's) gives payment access without the Fed's credit, and the proposed payment account would do something similar for a new class of firms. Without any account, a firm reaches the Fed only through a bank that has one.
search_context: fed-account-types grid banking

title: Who has a Federal Reserve account, and who is still waiting?
description: No crypto firm is confirmed to hold a full Federal Reserve master account. Kraken has a limited-purpose account; Anchorage Digital is waiting for a decision; Custodia Bank is fighting its denial in court.
search_context: fed-accounts line-up banking

title: What is each Reserve Bank studying in 2026?
description: Each Reserve Bank's 2026 conference records cover a different mix of topics. Across the six themes the library tracks, AI adoption and agentic controls is the widest (8 Banks: Boston, Cleveland, Richmond, Minneapolis, Dallas, San Francisco, New York, St. Louis); digital money, clearing and finality has 6; labor flows and regional distribution has 5; data governance and authority has 4; fraud, cyber and operational resilience has 4; power and physical infrastructure has 3 (Dallas, Minneapolis, San Francisco). Philadelphia falls under none of the six: its records are on mortgage transmission and intermediation. A conference topic shows what a Bank is paying attention to, not that it owns the function or has adopted a policy.
search_context: fed-bank-research grid banking

title: How big is FedNow now, and how fast is it growing?
description: FedNow settled 4,997,811 payments worth $274.664 billion in the second quarter of 2026 (54,921 a day), up from 2.7 million payments worth $271.3 billion in the first quarter. There were more than 1,800 live institutions by mid-July 2026 (about 1,600 in January), and the largest payment allowed rose from $500,000 at the July 20, 2023 launch to $1 million in March 2025 and $10 million in November 2025. The library holds only these two quarters of volume, so it cannot show a longer growth trend yet.
search_context: fed-fednow-size timeline banking

title: Can the President fire a Fed governor?
description: Only for cause, and only after notice and a chance to respond. On June 29, 2026 the Supreme Court (5-4) kept Governor Lisa Cook in office, holding that courts can review the 'cause' and that she got no notice or hearing. On October 7 the President set up a committee to try again, with a hearing set for November 5, 2026.
search_context: fed-governor-removal timeline banking

title: What did each House hearing on the Fed set out to change, and who testified?
description: The library records 11 House Financial Services hearings on the Fed, from March 4, 2025 to June 25, 2026: 9 by the Task Force on Monetary Policy and 2 by the full committee or a subcommittee. The Task Force heard 45 witnesses, and the library reads 12 of them as 'Analytical'; each card gives the witness's affiliation, a quote, and links to the committee memo and transcript.
search_context: fed-hearings timeline banking

title: Which Fed technology projects are live, and which are only proposed?
description: Of 17 Fed technology projects the library tracks, 9 are live (FedNow and its add-ons, the Reserve Banks' shared AI platform, Richmond's national IT, the New York repo platform, Philadelphia's collateral systems, Treasury central clearing and DTC's tokenized entitlements), 1 is an authorized but limited account (Kraken), 2 are scheduled (the 2027 FedNow discount and longer Fedwire hours in 2028 or 2029), 2 are proposals (the Payment Account and the Fed's stablecoin rules) and 3 are research only.
search_context: fed-technology line-up banking

title: Which licensed stablecoins outside the U.S. are actually live, and is their backing proven?
description: The library tracks 13 stablecoin products outside the U.S. 6 are live under a local license, and 4 of those publish regular attestations of their reserves (USDG · Singapore; XSGD · Singapore; XUSD · Singapore; Zand AED / AEDZ · United Arab Emirates). The rest are in beta, announced, used without a local license, or have no dated public proof of backing yet; the backing of 1 failed.
search_context: foreign-stablecoins line-up crypto

title: Where does each FORTRESS America base project stand on the proof ladder?
description: Of the 10 base projects the FORTRESS registry tracks, only MCAS Miramar microgrid has a public island test; 4 have public operating descriptions with different boundaries, 4 are at selection or negotiation, 1 is a prototype, and FORTRESS itself has no published site list, definition or funding yet.
search_context: fortress-ladder line-up force

title: What in Genesis is actually built and running, and what is still planned?
description: Of the 12 saved Genesis project profiles, 2 have a demonstrated workflow or partly operating services (OPAL and American Science Cloud/ModCon). NNSA has 1 authorized cloud environment, with Genesis workload deployment unproved. Another 4 are being built or designed, 4 are selected or planned, and 1 is consortium membership. The separate proposed Argonne center remains market research without a solicitation or award.

title: What are the 33 science challenges the Genesis Mission is meant to solve?
description: DOE's July 22, 2026 document lists 33 science and technology challenges in five areas: Protecting the Nation from Emerging Threats (9), Extending the Frontiers of American Discovery (8), Delivering Reliable Infrastructure and Energy Affordability (7), Building American Industrial Strength (5), Helping Americans Live Longer, Healthier Lives (4). They include 'Delivering Nuclear Energy That is Faster, Safer, Cheaper', 'Scaling the Grid to Power the American Economy', 'Software Understanding for National Security', 'Ensuring American Space Superiority'. All 33 are proposed objectives in DOE's text, not measured results; only 2 have a profiled Genesis project assigned: GridFM 2.0 (to 'Scaling the Grid to Power the American Economy') and Prometheus nuclear AI (to 'Delivering Nuclear Energy That is Faster, Safer, Cheaper').
search_context: genesis-challenges every record innovation

title: Which companies are Genesis members, which only pledged, and which have named project roles?
description: Of the 63 companies in the Genesis record, 46 are on the consortium's private-sector roster (checked October 13, 2026), 11 pledged support in October (5 of them without being on the roster), and 20 have a named role on a specific project.
search_context: genesis-companies line-up innovation

title: How much money is behind Genesis, and how much of it is real cash?
description: Genesis carries more than $5 billion in announced federal commitments, more than $800 million in partner support and $2.4 billion in October company pledges, but none of it is shown as cash paid: only 1 line includes obligated money, 2 are selections for award and 2 are open calls.

title: Who received the 278 Genesis project selections, and where are they?

title: When does the GENIUS Act take effect, and are any of its rules final?
description: The GENIUS Act takes effect on January 18, 2027. As of October 21, 2026, 1 of its rules is final and 12 are still proposals.

title: Which advisory boards, research centers and councils belong to, or advise, which federal agency?
description: The library has 102 checked relationships for 42 boards, councils and research centers across 28 agencies or offices. 19 are federally funded research centers, all run day to day by private operators (MITRE Corporation 6, RAND Corporation 4, Institute for Defense Analyses (IDA) 3); the rest are boards and councils that advise or are set up inside an agency. Being sponsored or supported is not being owned or controlled.

title: Where does the FY2027 budget request add or cut money, agency by agency?
description: The April request raises estimated federal outlays from $7,540.4 billion to $8,092.9 billion. Measured in base discretionary budget authority, the biggest increases are Defense Department (+28%) and Justice (+13%); the deepest cuts are Small Business Administration (-70%), National Science Foundation (-55%), Environmental Protection Agency (-52%). A request is not law: FY2027 is running on a continuing resolution through December 11, 2026.

title: Which federal bodies were created, cut, restructured or restored in 2025-26?

title: What has each congressional committee actually done in the 119th Congress, and which committees were never checked?
description: The library tracks 226 congressional committees and subcommittees of the 119th Congress. It has checked the calendars of 32; 194 were never checked, so a blank for them means not looked at, not idle. It holds 276 dated, officially verified outcomes for 19 of them (bills marked up, reported or passed, nominations, subpoenas and released transcripts), most from Committee on Oversight and Government Reform (101). The newest is from July 22, 2026.

title: In which institutions is control moving faster than legal responsibility?
description: The library tests 15 institutions for practical control running ahead of legal responsibility. The largest group (4) is 'authority contest': IMF surveillance & conditionality; Federal Reserve Payment Account; USAID legal survival / operating death; HHS / proposed AHA. The others: 3 operational test, 1 law ahead of complete operation, 1 proposed adaptation, 1 output shortfall, 1 mixed lag and contest, 1 positive-control candidate, 1 procedural test, 1 governance lag, and 1 positive control (Fedwire ISO 20022), where the legal operator and the records stayed intact. This is the library's lens, not a verdict.

title: Which Supreme Court money-case dates are coming up?

title: What has actually happened after an executive order was signed?

For the other orders the library has no dated record of what happened next, which is not the same as nothing happening.

title: Which Trump executive orders are still in force, and which were revoked, replaced or expired?
description: Of the 509 Trump executive orders on the library's record, 439 have no revocation on record in the library's reading (282 of the 288 second-term orders). 51 were revoked, 8 replaced by a later order, 2 partly replaced and 1 terminated; 5 had their operative date pass and 3 still wait for a Federal Register number. 72 rows carry a check flag.

title: Which parts of the national fraud-detection system are proven, and which are only announced or missing?
description: Of the 33 parts of the national fraud-detection system the library mapped, 18 are proved by a public record, 7 are announced with no public text, 2 are proposed and 2 are the library's inference. 4 are missing: Technical annex / SLA, NFDC system records, Collected recovery and Correction, notice and remedy path. Since the map, Treasury reported pre-payment verification fully operating on September 30, 2026.

title: How does a federal grant actually travel from Congress to a city, and what records prove each step?
description: Congress sets the purpose and budget authority, OMB apportions it, HUD makes the prime awards (for FY2024 HOME: $23,907,179 to New York's Housing Trust Fund Corporation and $1,303,112.35 directly to the City of Syracuse), Treasury's Fiscal Service pays, and auditors test afterward. title: How do catastrophe bonds and reinsurance carry disaster risk?
description: Alternative capital adds a funded layer to the reinsurance market. A sponsor transfers a defined risk to a special-purpose vehicle; investors fund collateral and receive a spread; a trigger can reduce principal or release collateral to the sponsor. The original insurer or public program normally remains the direct claimant-facing obligor. A hurricane, flood or earthquake is not itself the security trigger. For ordinary reinsurance the hub's rule is the same: ceded economics do not normally erase the original promise; cession ordinarily does not erase the direct insurer's policyholder obligation or prove that a recovery is due or collectible.

title: Who insures exporters and overseas investors against nonpayment or seizure?
description: Four kinds of risk bearer, in the study's map. For exporters: a private trade-credit insurer, which insures commercial or political nonpayment within limits and conditions, and EXIM export-credit insurance, which covers a stated share of eligible foreign-receivable nonpayment. For overseas investors: DFC political-risk insurance, which covers selected inconvertibility, expropriation, violence and contract risks, and the World Bank Group's MIGA guarantee and risk-sharing facility, which covers qualifying cross-border financing and may share first loss with donor or IDA resources. Export-credit insurance protects an exporter or lender against defined nonpayment. Political-risk insurance protects a qualifying investment or financing against named government or conflict risks. Neither makes the buyer's debt disappear, guarantees a country's currency value, covers physical cargo loss by default, or authorizes a transaction prohibited by sanctions.

title: When does the government pay for insurance losses, and after what trigger?

NFIP: federal primary flood-insurance program with contractors, reinsurance and borrowing. State catastrophe fund: statutory wholesale reimbursement layer. Guaranty association: limited post-impairment or insolvency protection. PBGC: federal limited guarantee for covered private defined-benefit pensions. An FHLBank advance is a secured liquidity loan from a government-chartered member-owned bank. Program authority and available capacity are not a paid federal claim.

title: What happens to your policy if your insurer fails?
description: A domestic insurer does not ordinarily enter the same federal bankruptcy process as an industrial company. State insurance law, the domiciliary commissioner and a supervising state court instead control conservation, rehabilitation or liquidation. Liquidation normally triggers the guaranty duty; financial distress alone does not. Coverage, limits, residency and product eligibility are state-law questions. The guaranty system does not make every creditor whole, insure the insurer, or convert failure into a federal bailout.

title: How do life insurers' promises turn into private credit and offshore reinsurance?
description: Policy and annuity money becomes long-dated liabilities that insurers invest: long promises supply investable general-account liabilities, and insurer asset allocation directs trillions into bonds, mortgages, structured assets and alternatives, including through a private credit and structured-asset channel. The issuing life insurer can then cede liabilities and economics to an asset-intensive reinsurer, secured by a trust, funds withheld or collateral. The NAIC's September 2026 analysis estimated $1.210 trillion of private-credit exposure at year-end 2025 after removing identifiable overlaps. The annual report says total ceded premium increased 32.8% to $580.5 billion and assumed premium increased 48.1% to $272.5 billion. Treasury convened state regulators in 2026 specifically around private credit, offshore reserve movement, RBC, private letter ratings and evolving business models. The hub's limit: Offshore location, reciprocal-jurisdiction status or large ceded reserve does not alone prove weakened security or insolvency.

Bermuda's listing is limited to named commercial and long-term insurer classes. Cayman is not listed in that document. The U.S.–EU agreement entered into force on April 4, 2018; the U.S.–UK agreement entered into force on December 31, 2020. In 2026 Treasury's Federal Insurance Office signed a memorandum with Bermuda's regulator and a cooperation statement with Cayman's; they are not covered agreements, reciprocal-jurisdiction designations, treaty approvals, licences or guarantees.

title: What changes when an employer moves its pension to an insurer?
description: Pension risk transfer changes the legal obligor and protection regime, not merely the asset manager. The chain differs for a buy-in, where the annuity remains a plan asset and the plan continues to owe participants, and a buy-out, where the insurer becomes the direct benefit payer for transferred obligations. PBGC also states that its guarantee ends after plan assets are distributed in a standard termination. The insurer becomes responsible for annuity payments. Any later state guaranty-association protection is state-, residency-, product- and limit-specific.

title: Who regulates insurers: states, Treasury, the Fed or global bodies?

Treasury's Federal Insurance Office monitors, advises, represents and administers bounded federal roles; the Financial Stability Oversight Council monitors system risk and can designate a nonbank under section 113; Federal Reserve insurance-group supervision applies only to covered holding companies and designated nonbanks. Global bodies write shared standards, but IAIS adoption is not self-executing state or federal law and does not itself intervene in a group.

title: Which Reserve Bank runs which national payment and Treasury service?

Boston runs FedNow; New York runs Fedwire Funds, Fedwire Securities and the National Settlement Service and carries out the Fed's open-market operations; Atlanta runs check and FedACH; Chicago runs FedLine access; Cleveland builds Treasury's Pay.gov; Minneapolis supports TreasuryDirect; Richmond hosts the System's national IT; Kansas City decides account requests.
search_context: reserve-bank-services map banking

title: When can an investment adviser hold clients' crypto keys itself under the SEC proposal?
description: Only as a last resort, and only if the proposal becomes final; the SEC proposed it on October 1, 2026 and no final rule has been issued. For an ordinary advisory client the rule reaches a crypto asset only when it is a fund or security. The adviser may hold the keys itself only when, after a written inquiry, no qualified custodian will hold that particular asset (cost does not count), re-checked at least quarterly, and it must move the asset to a custodian as soon as reasonably practicable once one is available. Only designated supervised people may hold key material, every movement needs at least two of them including a management person, and a technology vendor must not be able to reach the keys or move the assets alone, so a single-employee adviser cannot use the route.
search_context: sec-adviser-self-custody steps crypto

title: Which crypto technologies could fit the SEC's tokenized-stock exemption, and has anyone actually started?
description: Plenty could fit, but no one has started under the order. The library reads 20 core systems and 14 added ones against the ten seats an exempt venue needs: 4 are core technical candidates (Ethereum, Stellar, Solana, Algorand), 8 conditional candidates, 5 supporting layers and 3 outside the core design. The only public step so far is Imperium's filing as a prospective liquidity provider on September 28, 2026; it says it has not begun, and no venue notice or launch was found through October 5, 2026.
search_context: sec-exemption-technology grid crypto

title: What does the SEC's tokenized-stock exemption allow, and how big can it get?
description: SEC Release No. 34-106402, in effect September 17, 2026 through September 17, 2031, lets a qualifying U.S. tokenized securities venue trade tokenized versions of listed U.S. stocks in permissioned automated-market-maker pools on a public, permissionless blockchain without being an 'exchange', and lets firms supplying those pools with their own capital avoid 'dealer' status. Every pair must include a tokenized stock. Size is capped at 75 symbols and 0.25% of prior-month average daily volume for S&P 500, Russell 1000 and qualifying LULD ETPs (Tier 1), and 250 symbols and 2.5% for other eligible NMS stocks (Tier 2). It approves no venue, token or chain; custody, transfer-agent, clearing and settlement law still apply.
search_context: sec-tokenized-stock-exemption grid crypto

title: What does Securitize actually run, and which of its companies holds which license?
description: Securitize runs the official ownership record for tokenized funds and stocks, not the money. Through 6 separate companies it acts as an SEC-registered transfer agent, a broker-dealer with a trading system, an investment adviser, a fund administrator and an EU trading-and-settlement operator; each license belongs to that one subsidiary, not to the listed parent.
search_context: securitize entity chart crypto

title: Who can freeze, burn or block a stablecoin?
description: For 18 of the 36 crypto dollars here, the issuer can freeze or block coins, usually for suspected crime or on a court or government order. The GENIUS Act requires payment-stablecoin issuers to be able to do this.
search_context: stablecoin-freeze line-up crypto

title: Where does stablecoin interest go if the law bans paying it?
description: The GENIUS Act bars an issuer from paying holders interest just for holding the coin. 10 of the 17 issuers here say in their terms that holders get nothing, and 7 don't say. The interest earned on the reserves stays with the issuer, which shares much of it with distributors such as exchanges. Some of those distributors pay their own customers 'rewards', and whether that is allowed is the open question.
search_context: stablecoin-interest flow crypto

title: Can a stablecoin's issuer change while the coin, wallet and checkout stay the same?
description: Yes. Tether moved all of USD₮'s obligations to a new company effective January 27, 2025 without users changing wallets, and SoFi's current SOFID terms already allow a substitute issuer. PayPal moved its wallet customers to PayPal Digital on May 19, 2026, but Paxos stayed PYUSD's issuer. Circle's planned move to a New York issuer, Ripple's reserve bank and Fiserv's FIUSD programs are still plans. In each case the ticker, app and checkout can stay the same while the legal party behind them changes, so the proof is a signed transfer and new terms, not the app.
search_context: stablecoin-issuer-change line-up crypto

title: Who issues each dollar stablecoin, and who holds its reserves?
description: The library tracks 17 dollar coins that are, or want to be, payment stablecoins. Those with a cited size total about $271.6 billion, and USD₮ (USDT) and USDC are 94% of it. Reserves are mostly short-term Treasuries, Treasury repos, money-market funds and bank cash, held by a few large custodians named on each card.
search_context: stablecoin-issuers line-up crypto

title: Which states have made gold money or put bitcoin in a state reserve, and when does each take effect?
description: Gold, yes; bitcoin, not as money. Florida's gold-and-silver legal-tender law took effect July 1, 2026; in Texas, the law makes gold and silver specie legal tender from September 1, 2026, and the state's electronic gold currency may start no sooner than May 1, 2027. Louisiana (June 11, 2025, with a gold-payment registry added June 23, 2026) and Missouri (July 10, 2025) signed gold legal-tender laws whose start dates are not in the record. For bitcoin the rows show reserves, not money: New Hampshire and Arizona passed reserve laws in May 2025, Texas made the first state purchase on November 20, 2025, and Wisconsin's pension sold its stake. Every row is a reconstructed summary without an official link.

title: Which banks have used Swift's blockchain ledger, and for what?

title: What journal entries does each party book in a tokenized trade?
description: The entries follow the economic object, not the technology. At each step only the parties whose own books hold the cash, the security or the claim debit or credit anything; a token, a chain or a software provider books nothing by itself. The cards below print every entry, step by step.

title: When must U.S. Treasury trades be centrally cleared, and which clearinghouses can do it?
description: Under the SEC rule adopted December 13, 2023, eligible secondary-market Treasury cash trades must be centrally cleared by December 31, 2026, and repo by June 30, 2027; the SEC said in February 2025 it does not intend further extensions. Three clearinghouses are registered to do it: FICC (DTCC's subsidiary, the incumbent), CME Securities Clearing (registered December 1, 2025; its launch moved from Q2 to 'later in 2026') and ICE Clear Credit (its Treasury business approved January 30, 2026). The mandate does not apply to the Fed's own operations; clearing those is still only a proposal.
search_context: treasury-clearing timeline banking

title: What changes in central-bank digital money does the Library record?
description: The world record holds 25 dated moves on central-bank digital money in 10 regions, May 13, 2025 to July 1, 2026. It records moves, not a status, so each region below shows its latest move. Only two currencies have a stated status in a package: Japan's possible retail CBDC is 'pilot; not authorized' (September 15, 2026), and the UK digital pound is at grade M1, 'design decision pending' (September 14, 2026); a May 1, 2026 news report says it may be suspended instead, which is disputed and shown with both readings.
search_context: world-cbdc map world

title: Where is gold moving as money?
description: The world record holds 16 dated gold and reserve moves in 9 regions, January 30, 2025 to September 4, 2026. The newest that is not a social post: the PBoC reports its twentieth straight month of gold buying — 14.93 tonnes in June, the biggest monthly add since 2023, holdings near 2,346 tonnes. (China, July 7, 2026). Tonnages appear only inside each record's text; the master has no buy, sell or tonnage column.
search_context: world-gold map world

title: How do the IMF, the World Bank bodies and the BIS fit together, and where does the Fed connect?
description: Treasury speaks for the U.S. at the IMF and the five World Bank Group bodies (IBRD, IDA, IFC, MIGA, ICSID); the Fed Board is the U.S. member of the BIS. The Fed touches them at 5 points: U.S. policy seat; depositary and fiscal agent; SDR certificate chain; IMF surveillance; BIS membership. None of these gives the IMF or the Bank a say in Fed policy, or the Fed a vote inside them. Treasury's October 14, 2026 statement is a U.S. position, not yet a rule change at any of the institutions.
search_context: world-imf-worldbank-bis table world

title: How could the U.S. leave each international organization?
description: Each of the 27 bodies has its own exit route. Where the founding text names a period, it runs from immediately (Board of Peace) and on receipt of notice (International Monetary Fund) to 90 days (Organisation for the Prohibition of Chemical Weapons), six months (World Trade Organization, World Intellectual Property Organization), one year (NATO, OECD, International Civil Aviation Organization, International Maritime Organization, International Telecommunication Union) and two years (Organization of American States). For NATO the record adds: 'U.S. domestic statute requires Senate or Congress route'. 3 name a notice route without a period in the record (International Atomic Energy Agency, World Bank Group, ITER). 6 have no simple withdrawal clause (the United Nations Charter has none) and 4 are not memberships the U.S. could leave. 3 exits already carry a date: World Health Organization, UNESCO, Paris Agreement; the WHO exit, stated effective January 22, 2026, is disputed.
search_context: world-io-exit-routes line-up world

title: Is anything replacing the international bodies the U.S. is leaving?
description: Not wholesale: the registry counts 0 wholesale replacements among the 27 bodies (as of October 4, 2026). 17 bodies still do their job with no successor. 4 were left, given notice to leave, or reduced participation in with no successor at all: UN Human Rights Council, UNRWA, UNESCO, Paris Agreement. Only 3 show a changed default route, each for one bounded job: U.S. foreign health aid now goes through the America First Global Health Strategy bilateral network (the WHO's universal functions are retained); WTO appeals for participating non-U.S. Members go through the MPIA; and a U.S. side-by-side tax regime sits inside the OECD. Two pieces of new machinery exist (Artemis Accords, Board of Peace), and Kyoto Vision for a Golden Age of Science is doctrine only. The Board of Peace's Gaza field handoff was incomplete in September 2026. UNESCO remains under notice until December 31, 2026; pending departure is not effective exit.
search_context: world-io-successors entity chart world

title: Japan: which digital-money projects are at what stage?
description: On the Japan money map (as of September 15, 2026), 7 digital-money projects: DCJPY: bounded field test, JPYSC trust stablecoin: live, closed loop, Possible retail CBDC: pilot; not authorized, Project Agorá: controlled real-value test, Swift shared ledger: controlled initial use preparing, Indonesia–Japan QR corridor: production, Retired JGB–HKD DvP adapter: retired. Most still return to an existing bank, trust or Bank of Japan record; a retail CBDC has not been issued. The project map omits a reserve limit; the full saved Japan guide says up to half of issuance may move into qualifying short sovereign securities or term deposits.
search_context: world-japan-digital line-up world

title: Japan: if a bank or payment system fails, who takes the loss, in what order?
description: On the Japan money map (as of September 15, 2026), a failure moves through 5 separate steps: what sets it off (Ordinary liquidity stress, Operational outage, Systemic failure classification); the private first response (Commercial banks, Japan Securities Clearing Corporation, Zengin System and More Time, FMI default waterfalls); the Bank of Japan's liquidity step (BOJ Policy Board, BOJ current-account balances, BOJ-NET Funds Transfer System, BOJ Article 33 lending, BOJ Article 37 outage lending, BOJ Article 38 special support), which lends against collateral and does not cover a final loss; resolution (Cabinet and Prime Minister, Financial Services Agency, Deposit Insurance Corporation of Japan, TLAC and creditor loss, Deposit protection and transfer); and where the loss finally lands (Fraud compensation and restitution, JPYSC trust stablecoin, Possible retail CBDC, Industry contributions, Conditional fiscal subsidy or guarantee). Public money is a last, conditional step that needs legal and budget approval.
search_context: world-japan-loss steps world

title: Where do Korea's won stablecoin and Han River project stand?
description: The won stablecoin still has no law: the Korea country file says that as of October 3, 2026 South Korea had no enacted general public-won stablecoin regime, and that a future won stablecoin's issuer, reserves and redemption rules were unresolved. In the world money record, the Digital Asset Basic Act was introduced June 10, 2025, stalled December 30, 2025 over who may issue the token, the government proposed its own bill April 8, 2026, and on May 12, 2026 it was left off the National Policy Committee's last agenda before recess. The Bank of Korea paused Phase 2 of Project Han River (Hangang), its wholesale CBDC and tokenized-deposit trial with the banks, on June 26, 2025, and relaunched it March 18, 2026 with nine banks, retooled around tokenizing government disbursements; on July 1, 2026 the Bank floated growing it into foreign-bond investment infrastructure; and on July 15, 2026 its Phase II designation was expanded, with Kyongnam and iM Bank newly designated. The country file treats Hangang tokens as commercial-bank deposit claims in a controlled pilot; no public-won issuer or production wholesale CBDC was established.
search_context: world-korea-won timeline world

title: Which payment rails are being rebuilt around Swift, or alongside it?
description: The world record holds 35 dated payment-plumbing moves in 10 regions, January 6, 2025 to July 7, 2026: China's CIPS signing foreign banks, BRICS Pay targeted for a pilot, Africa's PAPSS, Indonesia's QRIS reaching Japan, Korea and China, Project Nexus, and the ECB's Pontes and Appia links. Swift's own shared ledger has four readings: announced September 29, 2025; 'controlled initial use preparing' on the Japan map (September 15, 2026); 'MVP ready; pilots pending', grade M4, on the UK map (September 14, 2026); and, newest, 17 listed banks and 6 bank-published bilateral pilot cases (October 19, 2026).

title: UK: which documents legally control a stablecoin, digital gilt or tokenised fund, and which are still missing?
description: Of 26 documents that control UK stablecoins, the digital gilt (DIGIT), tokenised funds and settlement (UK map, as of September 14, 2026), 10 are in force or final, 3 are drafts or open, and 13 are required but not published, not located or not yet inspected — among them the HSBC Gate 2 finality self-attestation, the DIGIT platform-provider appointment, the HSBC–LSEG bilateral DSD memorandum.

title: Who can make law for each part of the UK and its territories?
description: The UK Parliament can make law for the whole UK ('Parliamentary sovereignty within the UK constitutional order'). It has handed law-making for devolved matters to three legislatures: the Scottish Parliament (Scotland Act 1998 as amended), Senedd Cymru (Government of Wales Act 2006 as amended) and the Northern Ireland Assembly (Northern Ireland Act 1998 and Agreement settlement). England has no legislature of its own on the map: it is 'predominantly governed through UK institutions, local government and devolved local arrangements'. The 3 Crown Dependencies (Bailiwick of Jersey, Bailiwick of Guernsey, Isle of Man) and 14 British Overseas Territories are not part of the UK. The Crown Dependencies are self-governing under island constitutional law (Jersey answers to its States Assembly, the Isle of Man to Tynwald), linked through the Crown, with the Privy Council handling 'Royal Assent and specified Crown functions'. Each Overseas Territory runs under its own constitution or Orders within the UK constitutional framework, with a Governor or Commissioner; the map does not name each territory's legislature.
search_context: world-uk-lawmakers entity chart world

title: UK: how far has each on-ledger money, gilt or settlement project got?
description: Of 15 UK on-ledger money, gilt and settlement projects on the UK map (as of September 14, 2026), the furthest along is the Tokenised authorised-fund register at M7 (authoritative-record integration); 1 at M5 (limited production); 10 at M4 (authorised or production-bound); 2 at M1 (technical prototype or design work); 1 at M0 (concept or policy intention). The least advanced: HSBC–LSEG DSD link, Digital pound design phase, Bank of England Synchronisation Lab. No project has reached M8 or above (liquidity integration, proven failure and exit, normal infrastructure).
search_context: world-uk-ledger line-up world

title: Who runs the City of London and UK public money?
description: HM Treasury runs UK public money: it administers the UK Consolidated Fund, the National Loans Fund and the Debt Management Account and owns the Exchange Equalisation Account, the Bank of England and The Royal Mint; the Bank of England (whose capital is held for Treasury, with statutory independence) operates RTGS / CHAPS and acts as Treasury's agent for the Exchange Equalisation Account. Parliament legislates for 'tax, Supply and financial-services law', and the National Audit Office serves it. Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland each keep their own consolidated fund, answerable to their legislature. The City of London is run by the City of London Corporation, through the Court of Common Council and the Court of Aldermen; it keeps the City Fund, the City's Estate and the City Bridge Foundation separate, and it 'does not set UK tax, regulate UK finance or constitute a state within a state.' It is a different body from the Greater London Authority and the Mayor of London. 'The City' as a financial market is not a legal person: the FCA and the PRA regulate the firms in it.
search_context: world-uk-public-money entity chart world

title: How does a UN decision get made, paid for and carried out, and who controls each step?
description: A General Assembly decision passes through 13 steps, each with its own controller: Member States authorize; a state, organ or the Secretary-General asks for an agenda item; the General Committee filters it; a Main Committee takes the work; sponsors and co-facilitators write the text; the Assembly adopts it (two thirds for budget and other important questions, a simple majority otherwise); then the Fifth Committee and ACABQ decide the money, the Secretary-General carries it out, and auditors and Member States review it. Adoption is not funding, and funding is not delivery.
search_context: world-un-decisions steps world

title: Where does the UN's AI and digital-technology build-out stand?
description: Of the 12 layers the UNGA81 package tracks (as of September 30, 2026), 3 are operating (Mandate and focal point; Evidence, dialogue and implementation lab; Capacity centres and diffusion network), 6 are under way, 2 are proposed only and 1 is only a panel that was held. The money is not there yet: the Secretary-General proposes a $3 billion starting fund and the September 21 closed design session was held; no governing or capitalization instrument was located at cutoff. Cross-border AI sandboxes: the Valencia Lab operates and the September 21 co-design session was held, but no public charter, standards work item, shared-protocol network or pilot was located. Tokenization as public infrastructure: the September 21 panel was held; Pakistan publicly framed tokenization around remittances, SME finance, sovereign debt, access, safeguards and standards participation, while no UN standard, legal model or pilot was located.
search_context: world-un-tech-buildout line-up world

title: What did the 2026 UN General Assembly week actually produce?

The Durban anniversary declaration is past due: its meeting has passed and the library has no record of adoption. No AI fund, sandbox network or UN tokenization model was set up.

title: Which international bodies has the U.S. left, and when does each exit take effect?
description: Saved evidence through October 4, 2026. The U.S. has completed withdrawal from 1 treaty regime: the Paris Agreement (effective January 27, 2026). Its exit from the World Health Organization is claimed effective January 22, 2026 but disputed: WHO still treated the U.S. as a member in arrears in May 2026. UNESCO exit takes effect December 31, 2026. The parent UN climate treaty (UNFCCC) exit takes effect February 27, 2027. On February 3, 2025 it stopped taking part in the UN Human Rights Council and cut its money to UNRWA, without leaving the UN. For 10 other bodies an exit clause exists but no U.S. notice was found.

title: What does the U.S. pay, and how does it vote, in each international body?
description: The U.S. share runs from 49.99% (Organization of American States, 2026 assessed quota) down to 9.09% (ITER, construction sharing baseline). At the UN it pays 22% of the regular budget and 26.1371% of peacekeeping, but still has one Assembly vote. Paying more buys more votes only where votes are weighted by money, at the IMF and World Bank: the U.S. IMF share can block decisions requiring 85% of total voting power; IBRD influence derives from shareholding.

title: What can the U.S. block or decide in each international body, and what can't it?
description: Across 27 bodies, U.S. power sits in five different places: a veto, consensus seat or blocking share in 5 (United Nations, NATO, International Monetary Fund, ITER, Board of Peace), money leverage in 8, domestic implementation in 8, command or facility access in 5 and agenda power in 6. A gate can stop specified action but does not give command: at the UN Security Council, procedural matters require nine votes and are not vetoable; affirmative action still needs nine votes.

title: Who loses money if AI demand falls depends on each deal
description: AI infrastructure is financed through several separate structures (GPU funds, GPU loan vehicles, cloud companies, data-center property and power plants), so who owns the chips, who owes the debt and who takes the loss has to be traced one deal at a time.
search_context: Who owns the GPUs and other AI-infrastructure assets, who owes the debt, what cash flow services it, and who absorbs loss if utilization or residual value collapses? AI infrastructure capital stack GPU ownership debt obligor servicing cash flow residual value terminal loss GPU project finance NVIDIA GPU lease funds project SPVs AI-cloud operators data-center property owners power-equipment owners lenders customers

title: AI helps run turbines, but people still make the big calls
description: Turbines are run by layers of sensors, controls, monitoring centers, analytics and work-order systems. AI does narrow jobs now, such as inspection, spotting problems and small tuning loops, but no fleet is run by AI, and most newly ordered big gas turbines won't run until 2027 or later.
search_context: What technology is actually being used to manage turbine assets as the United States expands power infrastructure, how much is genuinely automated with AI, and how fast are the physical and digital buildouts moving? turbine asset management AI maintenance remote monitoring digital twin APM EAM CMMS gas turbine buildout power infrastructure U.S. power system gas turbine OEMs electric utilities EIA FERC PJM

Tokenization is an optional post-trade settlement-form flag: same CUSIP, symbol, order book, priority and fees; market data does not distinguish forms; settlement stays T+1. DTC decides eligibility, and anything ineligible falls back to traditional settlement. No operative start notice was located. About 11% of DTC participants were excluded per the 24X filing. 'The most important word is ... fungible.'

title: Far Overhaul Binding Rule Vs Class Deviation
description:
EO 14275 (Apr. 15, 2025, 90 FR 16447) orders the FAR cut back to what statute requires or what sound procurement still needs. OMB M-25-26 (May 2, 2025) splits the work into two clocks: **Phase I class deviations now**, **Phase II notice-and-comment later** under 41 U.S.C. § 1707.

Acquisition.gov issues model deviation text part by part. Agencies adopt it by class deviation. The FAR Companion and buying guides are **non-mandatory**. They are not the FAR.

FR Doc. 2026-12559, 91 FR 37550 (June 23, 2026), is **one of twelve proposed rules** (FAR Case 2026-001). Comments closed July 23, 2026. A final rule was **not retrieved at cutoff**.

EO 14402 pushes fixed-price as the default. EO 14398 writes a DEI-ban clause into contracts and calls compliance material for the False Claims Act. Neither order repeals Title 41. Neither order is the FAR.

This is the buying rulebook under the payment record. Defend the Spend can show a payment. It cannot show whether the award was made under the old FAR, a class deviation, or a rule that has not yet been issued.

title: Fed Payment Stack Control Finality And Clock Gap
description: There is no single payments stack but five control layers on different clocks. Findings: the clock gap (clearing, guarantee and token hours extend faster than securities-transfer and central-bank cash hours, so private prefunded liquidity bridges the gap); the access paradox (the proposed Payment Account is strictly prefunded, no credit, $1,000,000,000 closing cap); and the accounting-control gap (no application-level ledger).

title: Fisa 702 Split Clock State
description:
Two clocks.

**Clock 1 — the statute.** Title VII of FISA, including section 702 (50 U.S.C. § 1881a), is repealed **effective June 12, 2026**, except as provided in section 404 of the FISA Amendments Act of 2008. The repeal sits in FAA § 403(b), last amended by **Public Law 119-87** (Apr. 30, 2026). House OLRC prelim, text in effect August 14, 2026, still prints that date. No later enacted reauthorization was retrieved at cutoff.

**Clock 2 — the paper already issued.** FAA § 404(b)(1) (50 U.S.C. § 1801 note): any **order, authorization, or directive** issued under Title VII “shall continue in effect until the date of the expiration of such order, authorization, or directive.” Section 702 itself, while live, let the Attorney General and the DNI authorize targeting “for a period of **up to 1 year** from the effective date of the authorization.”

**H.R. 9238** would have moved the repeal from June 12, 2026 to July 2, 2026. The House **rejected** it on June 11, 2026: **198–218** on a motion to suspend the rules. Tracker: Failed House.

**FISC order not retrieved at cutoff.** The FISC public docket and ODNI/intel.gov releases do **not** contain a March 2026 (or nearby) section 702 certification opinion. No grandfather end date is written here.

The charter to start **new** 702 work is gone as of June 12. Paper already signed, if any still has time on it, is a different object.

title: Ieepa Emergency Powers Tariff And Blocking State
description:
*Learning Resources, Inc. v. Trump* and *Trump v. V.O.S. Selections, Inc.*, Nos. 24-1287 and 25-250 (Feb. 20, 2026), 607 U.S. ___:

> **Held:** IEEPA does not authorize the President to impose tariffs.

The Federal Circuit judgment against the tariffs (No. 25-250) is **affirmed**. The D.D.C. action (No. 24-1287) is **vacated and remanded with instructions to dismiss for lack of jurisdiction**. The tariff challenges belong on the CIT / Federal Circuit path.

Roberts, C.J., announced the judgment. Parts I, II–A–1, and II–B (the statutory holding that “regulate … importation” does not include the power to tax) are the opinion of the Court, joined by Sotomayor, Kagan, Gorsuch, Barrett, and Jackson. Parts II–A–2 and III (major-questions overlay) are Roberts, Gorsuch, and Barrett only. Kagan, joined by Sotomayor and Jackson, concurred in the judgment on ordinary statutory tools and would not have invoked major questions. Thomas dissented. Kavanaugh dissented, joined by Thomas and Alito. **Judgment 6–3.**

The list in 50 U.S.C. § 1702(a)(1)(B) is investigate, block, regulate, direct and compel, nullify, void, prevent or prohibit — acquisition, holding, use, transfer, importation, exportation, dealing in property. **“Absent from this lengthy list of specific powers is any mention of tariffs or duties.”** Had Congress meant the tariff power, it would have said so, as it does in the statutes that actually grant duties (Trade Expansion Act § 232; Trade Act § 301).

**Same day, operating paper.** EO 14389 (Feb. 20, 2026; 91 FR 9437): the additional **ad valorem duties imposed pursuant to IEEPA** in the listed 2025–26 emergency orders “shall no longer be in effect and, as soon as practicable, shall no longer be collected.” **The national emergencies remain.** Actions that are not those IEEPA duties remain. Section 232 and section 301 duties are **unaffected**. EO 14388 (de minimis suspension) is **unaffected**.

**Same day, different statute.** Proclamation **11012** (Feb. 20, 2026; 91 FR 9339): a 10 percent ad valorem surcharge under Trade Act § 122, 19 U.S.C. § 2132. The statute lets the President proclaim a surcharge **not exceeding 15 percent** for a period **not exceeding 150 days** unless extended by Act of Congress. The proclamation itself: goods entered or withdrawn for consumption on or after 12:01 a.m. EST **February 24, 2026**, through 12:01 a.m. EDT **July 24, 2026**, unless earlier ended or extended by Act of Congress. **No extending Act retrieved at cutoff.** That is not IEEPA. A later CIT judgment on 11012 is a different object, named below.

**Claim cut.** “IEEPA is dead” is **not established**. The tariff use is dead. The block/regulate/nullify machine is the statute Congress wrote. OFAC still runs on it.

title: Impoundment And Rescission Legal Map
description:
The purse has two doors. The fraud machine asks whether a payment should leave. This map asks whether appropriated money may be **unspent**.

The Impoundment Control Act of 1974 lets the President *propose* a rescission by special message and withhold the money for 45 calendar days of continuous session. The money "shall be made available for obligation unless, within the prescribed 45-day period, the Congress has completed action on a rescission bill." Only Congress can cancel the appropriation. That is 2 U.S.C. § 683(b).

Public Law 119-28, signed 2025-07-24, is that bill for the June 3 2025 special message. It is an enacted rescission. The August 28 2025 special message is a later § 683 proposal — 15 items, $4.9 billion as the Federal Register notice itself states. It is not P.L. 119-28. Calling it a "pocket rescission" is the sender's theory. GAO B-330330 (2018) holds the ICA does not permit withholding through the date the money expires.

EO 14215 § 5 is the quiet twin: OMB may adjust independent-agency apportionments, including a bar on spending particular activities, "so long as such restrictions are consistent with law." Apportionment is not a rescission.

title: Iran War Powers Authority State
description:
No 2026 Iran declaration of war. No enacted Iran AUMF. **H.J. Res. 176** (Barrett) is introduced only — referred to House Foreign Affairs 2026-05-07. It is not law.

The President directed force on **2026-02-28** and sent Congress a written report dated **2026-03-02** (printed as **H. Doc. 119-139**). That letter rests on **Article II** (Commander in Chief and Chief Executive). It does **not** cite the 2001 AUMF, the 2002 AUMF, or any other statute as the force grant. Later 2026 letters (June 12, June 29, July 10, August 3) again cite Article II and say they are “consistent with” the War Powers Resolution. They do not enact authority.

**H. Con. Res. 86** is the only 2026 Iran instrument **agreed by both chambers**. House **215–208** (2026-06-03, Roll 199). Senate **50–48** (2026-06-23, Vote 184). Enrolled the same day. It is a **concurrent** resolution under WPR **§ 5(c) / 50 U.S.C. § 1544(c)**. A concurrent resolution is **not presented** to the President. It is **not** a public law. It cannot be vetoed because it never reaches the desk.

No later **joint** resolution directing removal was presented, vetoed, or enacted. Senate discharge votes on the joint-resolution path (**S.J. Res. 172, 180, 181, 184**; motion on **S.J. Res. 185**) all **failed**. **H.J. Res. 156** (clock-compliance joint resolution) is introduced only.

**Claim cut.** “Congress ended the war” is **not established**. What is established: both chambers **expressed** a § 5(c) direction, without a veto-proof statute, without presentment, and without an enacted AUMF.

**The 60-day clock result is not computed here.** § 1544(b) runs only from a report **submitted or required under § 1543(a)(1)** (hostilities). The March 2 letter’s **text** does not name a subsection. The **GPO/House header** on H. Doc. 119-139 classifies the communication under **§ 1543(a)(3)** (substantial enlargement) and **§ 1543(b)** — not (a)(1). Barrett’s **unenacted** recitals say the sixty days have expired. Those recitals are not a court finding and not a statute.

title: Title 10 Guard And Insurrection Act Authority State
description:
The President federalized Guard under **10 U.S.C. § 12406**. He did **not** invoke the Insurrection Act, **10 U.S.C. §§ 251–255**. No § 254 proclamation to disperse was retrieved.

*Trump v. Illinois*, No. 25A443 (Dec. 23, 2025), **denied** the Government’s stay. The unsigned order held that “regular forces” in § 12406(3) “likely refers to the regular forces of the United States military.” Because the President had not invoked a statute that excepts the Posse Comitatus Act, 18 U.S.C. § 1385, the Government had not carried its burden to show that § 12406(3) lets him federalize the Guard to protect federal personnel and property in Illinois. The Court did **not** decide the Insurrection Act. Justice Kavanaugh said so in footnote 2 of his concurrence.

Vault notes that say “SCOTUS greenlit the Insurrection Act” name a different object. The order leaves that statute unused and the Illinois deployment barred at the stay stage.

title: Universal Relief After Trump V Casa
description:
On June 27, 2025 the Supreme Court, per Justice Barrett, held that **universal injunctions likely exceed the equitable authority Congress gave the federal courts in the Judiciary Act of 1789.** The Court granted the government's applications for partial stays of three preliminary injunctions against EO 14160, "but only to the extent that the injunctions are broader than necessary to provide complete relief to each plaintiff with standing to sue."

The applications "do not raise — and thus the Court does not address — the question whether the Executive Order violates the Citizenship Clause or Nationality Act." That sentence is load-bearing. *CASA* did not decide birthright. *Barbara* did, a year later.

What remains open, because the Court said so: APA vacatur, nationwide class relief under Rule 23, and how wide "complete relief" runs when the plaintiff is a State. A single district judge no longer freezes the whole country for non-parties. That changes the operating clock of every later order on the EO spine.

description: The Fed's role is a statutory operating arrangement created by Congress, not a private agreement or surrender of sovereignty.
